explanations.answer: God's promise has given him life
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. He says, "This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life." Notice he doesn't say the trouble got fixed first. I think a comfort that doesn't wait for the trouble to leave is the kind you can carry around in your apron pocket.

explanations.answer: His enemies have finally gone quiet
explanations.explanation: Quiet enemies would be lovely, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. What he says is, "This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life." His comfort is that God's promise has given him life.

explanations.answer: His friends have stayed close by
explanations.explanation: Friends are a gift, but this verse doesn't mention them. He says, "This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life." So what comforts him is that the promise has given him life, and I think that's a big deal.

Not quite, baker, and I'm glad, because the text says the opposite. The arrogant utterly deride him, "…but I do not turn from Your law." Mocked to the max and he still doesn't budge. I'd have crumbled faster than a day-old cookie.
Right, he doesn't turn away. He says, "The arrogant utterly deride me, but I do not turn from Your law." That "but" is doing a lot of heavy lifting. The mocking comes in, and the law stays put.

Yes, friend. He says, "I remember Your judgments of old, O LORD, and in them I find comfort." He remembers the judgments of old and finds comfort in them. Some people scroll for comfort, and he remembers.
That would be a natural thing to long for, but it's not what he says here. He finds comfort in remembering "…Your judgments of old, O LORD…" The memory is about God, not about his easier days.
No teachers show up in this verse, baker. What he remembers is the LORD's judgments of old, and he says he finds comfort in them. Good thing to check the verse itself before picking an answer.

That's it. He says, "Rage has taken hold of me because of the wicked who reject Your law." It's strong language, and the text doesn't soften it. What sets him off is people turning their backs on God's law.
Study isn't the word, friend. The verse says rage has taken hold of him because of the wicked who "…reject Your law." Rejecting is the word the psalmist uses.

If they kept God's law, I don't think he'd be enraged. Later he says he is a friend to those who keep God's precepts (Psalm 119:63). The verse says the wicked reject it, and that's why rage takes hold of him.

Yep, baker. The psalmist says, "Your statutes are songs to me in the house of my pilgrimage." He says God's statutes are songs to him, right there in the house of his pilgrimage. I hum while I stamp, and my mustache sways along.
Chains is a heavy word, baker, and he doesn't use it. He says God's statutes are songs to him. Later he says he delights in God's law (Psalm 119:70), and nobody delights in chains.
He does ask God to teach him the statutes (Psalm 119:64), but he doesn't call them riddles. In this verse, they are songs to him. Songs you can sing even when you're far from home.
Correct. He says, "In the night, O LORD, I remember Your name, that I may keep Your law." Most of us remember an embarrassing thing from 2009 at 3 a.m. He remembers the LORD's name.

The text says it's true, friend. Here is what the verse says: "In the night, O LORD, I remember Your name, that I may keep Your law." So it isn't false. The night is when he remembers God's name, and the verse gives the reason: that he may keep God's law.

You got it, baker. "This is my practice, for I obey Your precepts." The reason he gives is that he obeys, with no long speech attached. Me, I need three paragraphs to explain why I'm late to my own bakery.
The verse doesn't say a word about his family, baker. The reason he gives is, "…I obey Your precepts." I won't add a reason the text doesn't give.

Enemies do show up in this stretch, but they aren't the reason here. He says, "This is my practice, for I obey Your precepts." The reason he gives is that he obeys, not that anybody is watching. If the reason were an audience, I think it'd be a shaky one, and the verse doesn't use it.

That's right, baker. The verse says, "The LORD is my portion; I have promised to keep Your words." Those two things sit side by side in the same verse. He calls the LORD his portion, and he says he has promised to keep God's words.
No altar comes up in this verse, friend. He says, "I have promised to keep Your words." Building is a fine thing, but it's not the promise here.
A tenth isn't mentioned in these verses. What he promises is to keep God's words. That's the promise sitting right next to "The LORD is my portion…"

Other way around, baker. The psalmist says he has sought God's face with all his heart. That's the full heart, every bit of it, and no halves anywhere in the verse. Then he asks God to be gracious to him according to His promise.
Right, that one's false. He tells God he has sought His face with all his heart, no half measures. Then he asks for grace according to God's promise. That's a man who gave it his all, baker.
That's it, baker. "I considered my ways and turned my steps to Your testimonies." He considers his ways, and then he turns his steps to God's testimonies. I like that the considering comes first.
The text sends his steps somewhere else, friend. He says, "I considered my ways and turned my steps to Your testimonies." His own plans don't come up.

explanations.answer: To the ways of the nations
explanations.explanation: The nations aren't in this verse, baker. After considering his ways, he turned his steps to God's testimonies. That's where he points his feet.
Nope, no taking his time here. He says, "I hurried without hesitating to keep Your commandments." Me? I can hesitate ten minutes over which sprinkles to use.
Right, baker, it's false. The psalmist says, "I hurried without hesitating to keep Your commandments." He hurried, and the verse adds that he didn't hesitate. Taking his time is not what he says.

Yes, baker. "At midnight I rise to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments." He rises at midnight, and thanks is what he rises for. The thanks is for God's righteous judgments. That's one thankful man.

The verse doesn't say that, friend. He rises at midnight "…to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments." Praying for enemies doesn't appear in this verse. I can barely get up for my own timer, so a midnight thank-you impresses me.
Close to the theme, but not what the verse says. He says, "At midnight I rise to give You thanks for Your righteous judgments." He rises for thanks.

Yes, baker! He says, "I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts." He is a friend to the people who fear God and keep His precepts. I think a table with friends like that has room for one more chair.

Close, because he does call himself God's servant in the next stretch (Psalm 119:65). But toward those who fear God and keep His precepts, he says he's a friend. Servant is how he speaks about himself to the LORD.
Stranger isn't it, baker. He says, "I am a friend to all who fear You, and to those who keep Your precepts." A friend, not a stranger.

Correct, baker. He says, "The earth is filled with Your loving devotion, O LORD; teach me Your statutes." The whole earth is full of it. And right after saying so, he asks God to teach him His statutes.
The text says it's true, friend. He says, "The earth is filled with Your loving devotion, O LORD…" The whole earth, filled up.

Correct, baker. "Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in Your commandments." He asks to be taught, and he gives the reason that he believes in God's commandments. The request and the reason come together in one verse. Asking to learn is a good habit at any age.
The text says it's true, baker. He says, "Teach me good judgment and knowledge, for I believe in Your commandments." His request comes with a reason: he believes in them.
Yes, he's honest about it. "Before I was afflicted, I went astray…" Nobody likes admitting that. I once tried to stamp a cookie upside down, so I know the feeling.
The verse says something else, friend. He says, "Before I was afflicted, I went astray…" Home isn't mentioned.
No king appears in this verse, baker. What he says about before he was afflicted is, "…I went astray…" He's looking at his own path.
That's the opposite of what the text says, friend. He says, "but now I keep Your word." No struggling mentioned. It's a contrast with going astray before.
Right. Before he was afflicted he went astray, "but now I keep Your word." Now he keeps it. He doesn't say he struggles.
That's it, baker. "Their hearts are callous and insensitive, but I delight in Your law." Callous hearts on one side, and delight on the other. Delight is the word he picks for his own heart.
Hiding isn't what he says, baker. The verse says, "…I delight in Your law." Delight is the word he uses, set against the callous hearts of the arrogant.
Wavering isn't in this verse, friend. The arrogant have callous hearts, "…but I delight in Your law." Delight is the word.

explanations.answer: So he might learn God's statutes
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes." He doesn't say the affliction itself was fun. He says it was good for him, and he gives the reason. The reason is that he might learn God's statutes.

explanations.answer: So his enemies would leave him
explanations.explanation: The verse gives a different reason, friend. He says it was good "…that I might learn Your statutes." His enemies leaving isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: So he could rest from his work
explanations.explanation: Rest doesn't come up here, baker. He says, "It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes." Learning is the reason.

explanations.answer: Thousands of pieces of gold and silver
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. He says, "The law from Your mouth is more precious to me than thousands of pieces of gold and silver." The comparison is with thousands of pieces of gold and silver. He calls the law more precious to him than all of that.

explanations.answer: A king's crown and all his jewels
explanations.explanation: That sounds fancy, friend, but it's not what he says. He says the law is more precious to him than "…thousands of pieces of gold and silver." No crown in this verse.

explanations.answer: Herds of cattle and fields of grain
explanations.explanation: Cattle and grain aren't in the verse, baker. He weighs the law from God's mouth against "…thousands of pieces of gold and silver." And the law is more precious.
